title: Athanasius (c. 296–373)
hook: exiled again and again, he held that Christ is truly God

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pachomius, the soldier who gathered monks under one wall and one rule. Your line was together in the desert. Who worked beside you? Day seven hundred twenty-two.

Night, in a church in Alexandria. The people are keeping vigil with their bishop. Outside, soldiers surround the building, and then they break in. In his own account of that night, the bishop doesn't bolt for the back door. He stays in his chair. He tells the deacon to begin a psalm, and the people answer the refrain, for his mercy endureth for ever, while they slip out ahead of him. Only when most are safe does he slip away himself, into the dark. His name is Athanasius, and it isn't the first time he's had to run.
screen: `SOLDIERS AT THE DOORS.` → `HE STAYS IN HIS CHAIR.` → `THE PSALM KEEPS GOING.`

segments.voice: First, who he was: bishop of Alexandria, a great city of the early Church, in an age when emperors had begun to take a close interest in what bishops taught. Athanasius held one thing with his whole life: that Jesus Christ, the Son, is truly God, not the highest of creatures but one in being with the Father. Tomorrow we'll meet the argument on the other side. Today, the man who wouldn't move. Second, what it cost him. Emperors sent him away, and sent him away again. He was exiled to distant cities. He hid in the desert among the monks, who kept him safe, and, tradition says, once in his own father's tomb. He came back each time and took up his work, writing letters and books from wherever he was. Third, why it mattered so much to him. In his little book On the Incarnation, he gives the reason in a single sentence: "He was made man that we might be made God." If the Son were only a creature, Athanasius argued, he couldn't join us to God, because he would be on our side of the line too. Only God could bring us to God. The Catechism of the Catholic Church still quotes that line. Fourth, the phrase in today's carry. Later generations summed him up in Latin: Athanasius contra mundum, Athanasius against the world. It's a saying about him, not a slogan he chose. And it can be misheard as stubbornness for its own sake. For Athanasius, the point was never to win. It was to keep handing on what the Church had confessed, even while it was unpopular, and even when it meant sleeping in the desert. Catholics honor him as a saint and a Doctor of the Church.
screen: `BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA.` · `EXILED, AND EXILED AGAIN.` · `MADE MAN, THAT WE MIGHT BE MADE GOD.` · `A SAYING ABOUT HIM.` · then, large: `ATHANASIUS AGAINST THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find a truth you keep quiet about. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you hold to be true, about faith, about fairness, about a person, that you don't say out loud because it would cost you a little. Hold it. Don't rehearse an argument. Ask a gentler question: what would it look like to stand by this, kindly, without needing to win? If you pray, you can ask God for courage and for gentleness together. The bell holds the time.
Athanasius. The bishop of Alexandria who, through exile after exile, held that Christ is truly God. Today's word.
Your line: athanasius against the world. Today, when something true is unpopular in the room, say it once, calmly, and let it stand. Day seven hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Athanasius as a bishop and Doctor of the Church, and his teaching that the Son is one in being with the Father is professed in the Creed at Sunday Mass.

notes: Index hook says 'exiled five times'; under the claims rule the script and its hook field give no count ('exiled again and again'). Keeper may restore the number with a source.

Hook follows Athanasius's own account (Apologia de fuga 24) of the night raid on the church: seated on his throne, deacon reading the psalm with the refrain 'for his mercy endureth for ever' (Ps 135/136), people leaving first. The refrain is phrased in Douay-Rheims style but not marked as a quotation; confirm.
'Tradition says, once in his own father's tomb' is from later church historians (Socrates/Sozomen); hedged. Confirm or cut.
On the Incarnation 54 quotation from Archibald Robertson's translation in Schaff's NPNF series (1892); confirm exact wording ('For He was made man that we might be made God').
CCC 460 quotes Athanasius on the Son becoming man so that we might become God; confirm reference.
'Athanasius contra mundum' is a later saying; confirm attribution phrasing.
Title dates are the index's; no dates in voice. Original left null on purpose.
